A unicycle is a vehicle that has only one wheel. The rider sits on top of it and pedals to move forward or backward.

That's the heart of it — one wheel, one rider, no engine.

Picture a bicycle. Now remove the front wheel, the handlebars, the chain, and the gears. What you're left with — a single wheel with a seat directly above it — is essentially a unicycle.

Its parts are simple:

  • One wheel — the only wheel the vehicle has
  • A short metal frame — sits just above the wheel
  • A saddle (the seat) — mounted on top of the frame, where the rider sits
  • Two pedals — attached directly to the centre of the wheel (the axle)

There are no handlebars. The rider's hands are free.

The pedals connect directly to the axle — the rod that runs through the centre of the wheel. When you push the pedals with your feet, the wheel turns. Push forward, the wheel rolls forward. Push backward, the wheel rolls backward.

One important detail: you cannot coast on a standard unicycle. On a bicycle, you can stop pedalling and still glide forward. On a unicycle, the pedals and the wheel are locked together — if the wheel is turning, so are the pedals, always. The moment you stop pedalling, the wheel stops too.

This is what makes a unicycle famous — and difficult.

A bicycle stays relatively stable because it has two wheels spread across a length. A unicycle has only one contact point with the ground. This means it has no built-in stability at all. It will fall over the moment the rider stops actively balancing.

Riding a unicycle requires the rider to constantly make tiny adjustments — leaning slightly forward to prevent falling backward, leaning slightly backward to prevent falling forward, and shifting body weight left and right to stay upright. The rider also uses the pedals to control speed and balance simultaneously.

This constant, active balancing is a learned skill. Most people take weeks or months of regular practice to ride one confidently.
Who Rides a Unicycle, and Why

Circus and street performers are the most iconic users. Because riding a unicycle already looks impressive to most people, performers use it as a base for even more dramatic tricks — juggling while riding, riding in circles, spinning in place, or riding an extremely tall unicycle (called a giraffe unicycle, which uses a chain to connect the pedals to the wheel, allowing the seat to be several feet in the air).

Sport and hobby riders form a large community worldwide. There are unicycle sports such as:

  • Unicycle hockey — played like ice hockey but on a gym floor, on unicycles
  • Mountain unicycling (MUni) — riding off-road on rugged terrain, on a unicycle built with a thick, sturdy wheel
  • Unicycle trials — an obstacle-course sport where riders jump over and balance on objects
  • Unicycle racing — timed races on flat tracks

Casual learners also ride unicycles simply as a hobby or fitness activity.

Not all unicycles look the same. There are several variations built for different purposes:

  • Standard / freestyle unicycle — the classic design, used for learning, tricks, and performances. Wheel size is typically around 20 inches in diameter.
  • Touring / commuter unicycle — has a larger wheel (often 29 or 36 inches) to cover distance more efficiently. Some people actually commute on these.
  • Mountain unicycle (MUni) — has a wide, knobby tyre built for rough terrain, similar to a mountain bike tyre.
  • Giraffe unicycle — a tall unicycle where the rider sits much higher than usual. It uses a chain drive (like a bicycle) to connect the pedals to the wheel, allowing the seat to be raised dramatically.
  • Electric unicycle (EUC) — a modern invention. This is a motorised, self-balancing wheel with footrests on the sides. It uses gyroscopic sensors and a motor to keep itself upright, so the rider doesn't have to pedal — they just lean to steer and control speed. While it shares the name "unicycle," it works very differently from a traditional unicycle.
How a Unicycle Differs from Similar Things

ConceptNumber of WheelsPedalsHandlebars
  • A bicycle has two wheels, a chain, handlebars, and usually a freewheel (you can coast). A unicycle has one wheel, no chain (usually), no handlebars, and no coasting.
  • A tricycle has three wheels and is very stable. A unicycle has one wheel and is inherently unstable.
  • A scooter has two wheels and an engine or a foot-push mechanism. A unicycle is human-powered via pedals.

You might hear or read the word "unicycle" used in a few ways:

  • "She can ride a unicycle — she learned it in circus school." — straightforward noun use.
  • "He was juggling on a unicycle in the town square." — refers to the vehicle being ridden during a performance.
  • "I tried to ride a unicycle once and fell off immediately." — the word used casually to describe the vehicle and the difficulty of learning it.

The word is also sometimes used figuratively to describe something that is difficult to keep balanced or that requires unusual skill to manage — though this is informal and not its primary meaning.
A unicycle is a one-wheeled, human-powered vehicle with a seat and pedals, known for requiring constant active balance from the rider, and used in performance, sport, and recreation.
